newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-European stocks end strong, lifted by U.S..
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-European stocks end strong, lifted by U.S..

text.p: European bourses ended sharply higher on Thursday, with British and German shares scoring record highs with help from another jump on Wall Street after a smaller-than-expected rise in U.S. nonfarm payrolls.
But the jobs data had a dampening effect on the dollar, which slipped to its session lows against the mark and yen.

U.S. June payrolls rose by 217,000, slightly less than the 222,000 analysts had predicted. The jobless rate rose to 5.0 percent from 4.8 percent and average hourly wages, often used as an inflation gauge, edged up to $12.22 from May's $12.18.
"There's nothing in these numbers that argues for a (Federal Reserve) tightening," said Mike Malpede, analyst at Refco.

The Federal Reserve's policy-making body decided on Wednesday to leave U.S. rates steady, but analysts expect higher rates later this year to keep a lid on inflation as the U.S. economy continues to grow strongly.
However, traders said a rate increase at the next policy-making meeting in August was less likely since growth seemed to be moderating at a high but sustainable, low inflation, pace.
U.S. bond prices rallied on the jobs data, sending longer-term rates sharply lower. The two- and 30-year yields dropped to the lowest since February.
As U.S. rates fell, the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed more than 100 points at the open to a record high before profit-taking swept the index off its peak.
European shares tracked the U.S. moves, with London's FTSE-100 and Frankfurt's DAX index scoring record high closes just below all-time intraday highs.
The FTSE's surge was Europe's most dramatic on Thursday, rising from more than 50 points down at the open on interest rate jitters to more than 100 up at its afternoon peak on the U.S. jobs data.

Bullish momentum sparked by the U.S. employment report shunted aside for now early fears British rates would rise sharply in coming months. After Britain's soft budget late on Wednesday, traders predicted the Bank of England would raise base rates at least 25 basis points at next week's meeting, the first in a series of expected rate increases.
On the DAX, SPAR AG was among the biggest gainers, jumping to its year high of 60.50 marks before settling up six at 59.

The electronically-traded German IBIS DAX index broke a key level at 3,900 for the first time in afterhours trade with Wall Street's help. It also closed just off its intraday record high of 3,944.34. Traders were setting their sights on 4,000 within the next few weeks.
France's CAC-40 index closed up nearly one percent. Traders were eyeing a move to 3,000 before consolidating gains and then another move upwards.
The U.S. monthly jobs report overshadowed the weekly figures released at the same time. Weekly jobless claims rose to 337,000 in the latest week from 332,000.

U.S. May housing completions, the Economic Cycle Research Institute's (ECRI) monthly future inflation gauge and the Center for International Business Cycle Research's (CIBCR) monthly leading inflation index released after the jobs figures had little market effect. Housing completions fell 6.5 percent to a 1.372 million annual rate, the ECRI gauge rose to 11.0 from May's revised 110.8 and CIBCR's June index fell to 104.7 from May's revised 105.2.
Traders expected markets to be relatively quiet on Friday with U.S. markets closed for the Fourth of July holiday.
CURRENCIES AT THE CLOSE
The dollar was at 113.45 yen and 1.7495 marks compared with 114.44 and 1.7515 in late Europe on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT THE CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index ended up 80.3 points at 4,831.70.
PARIS - The CAC-40 ended up 27.53 at 2,936.98.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed up 32.63 at 3,887.39 and the IBIS DAX was up 72.20 at 3,939.73.
PRECIOUS METALS
London gold closed at $331.50 an ounce, down from $332.35 at Wednesday's close, after Australia's central bank said it sold 167 tonnes of gold. Silver finished at $4.65.
